title: Prompt Caching
markdown:
The Executive system prompt is partitioned for Anthropic prompt caching by `openexecutive.prompts.cache_manager.build_system_blocks`. It emits at most two `cache_control` blocks, consolidated down from four to stay within Anthropic's 4-block API limit alongside the tool definitions and the agent loop's intra-turn marker.

- **Block 0 — persona + knowledge (1h TTL, always present):** the executive persona constant — `EXECUTIVE_PERSONA_PROMPT` for a team, `EXECUTIVE_PERSONA_SOLO_PROMPT` in solo mode — or an admin override, which wins as-is in either mode, with the `{VOICE_PERSONA}` substitution, then the admin's Council **additional instructions** for the Executive (`persona_instructions`, wrapped in `<additional_instructions>`; blank leaves the block byte-identical, and like the override it changes only on save), conditional `WEB_SEARCH_ADDENDUM` / `MCP_ADDENDUM`, the constant `TOOL_BUILDING_ADDENDUM` (when to build a tool with `run_script`, check `list_saved_tools` first, keep what will be needed again, and talk about it without saying "script"; present with a gateway unless `CHAT_SCRIPTS=false`, a setting, so constant per deployment), the identity addendum (exec name/email, impersonation guard), the *Connected Systems* section (whose Google part is derived from what the Google server is started with, `WORKSPACE_MCP_TOOLS` and `WORKSPACE_MCP_TOOL_TIER` as the MCP config sets them, and whose Microsoft 365 and synced-folder lines come from that config and settings; all are fixed until the config changes, so it is as cacheable as the rest), the constant `DELEGATION_ADDENDUM` while anyone on the install has Act as me on, the timezone addendum, and `KNOWLEDGE_INDEX_SUMMARY`. The timezone addendum names the user's zone, read fresh on every build from the workspace settings (`memory.workspace_settings.get_user_timezone`: the workspace's zone, else `USER_TIMEZONE`, else UTC). Every component is a constant or changes only when an admin or the user changes a setting, so the TTL is long. Setting a new time zone changes the addendum, so the 1h block misses once on that change and is warm again from the next turn — accepted, since a stale zone would mis-schedule follow-ups. Act as me works the same way: its addendum is keyed on the install-level setting (`delegation.settings.block0_delegation_on`), never on the turn or the speaker, so switching it on or off misses the 1h block once; off, block 0 is byte-identical to an install without the feature.
  The *Connected Systems* section (`prompts.connected_systems.render_connected_systems`) tells the model what is connected so it never has to discover it: Google Workspace on or off (on only when `google_workspace` is among the servers the running gateway started with, `MCPGateway.server_names`, so a gateway that failed to start never reads as connected; and *needs reconnecting* instead of connected while the server is in `MCPGateway.needs_reconnect` — set when a Google tool answers with an authorization failure such as `invalid_grant` (`mcp_gateway.grant_failure`), cleared by the next answer that is not one or by `mark_reconnected` — so the model stops promising mail it cannot read; the set changing re-renders block 0 and costs one cache miss), and when on, how to act from its own account plus the pinned Google tool names by service (`GOOGLE_TOOL_MANIFEST`: Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets, as workspace-mcp 2.4.2 names them) to call directly; any other configured MCP servers by name (`_comment` keys skipped); Slack / Discord / Telegram / Google Chat on or off from their settings (names only, never a token); Notion knowledge sync; a Confluence knowledge sync line only when that sync is on (a setting, so constant per deployment); and one constant Act as me line that points at `DELEGATION_ADDENDUM`, so switching Act as me still changes block 0 by that addendum alone. The "never ask which address to send from" guidance lives here now, shown only while Google is connected; the identity addendum keeps the name, address and impersonation guard. Every input is fixed per process and the output is sorted, so block 0 stays warm; it is appended even under a persona override. It replaces what the model used to learn from `search_tools`, an uncached proxy whose results were gone by the next turn.
- **Block 1 — company + org (5m TTL, only if non-empty):** `company_profile.to_prompt_block()` plus `render_org_block(mode=…)` — for a team: departments, heads, principals, charters and the People roster; in solo: the principal's own line, their role lines when set (a static lead-in marking the role private to the principal, then kind in plain words, title, reports to, remit, measured on — from the role pinned for the turn: the workspace settings, or a session's `principal_role` override), and their goals grouped by area, then the goals with no area under `### No area`. In both modes a goal with no department renders with its `goal_id` (a team's under `## Goals With No Department`), and a goal with an owner of its own names that owner. The role is set once per install and changes only when the principal edits it, so it is as stable as the rest of the block. Shorter TTL so org edits propagate quickly. The principal's contacts are private to them, so `build_system_blocks(include_contacts=...)` adds the `## Contacts` section, after the team or solo block, only on the principal's own verified turn (`executive._contacts_in_prompt`). That gives block 1 exactly two stable variants per mode — with and without contacts — and never anything per-request; every other turn's block is byte-identical to an install with no contacts.

## Solo mode: one prefix per mode

Solo mode — one person using Open Executive for themselves — changes three cached parts, all resolved **once per turn** by `pin_turn_workspace_mode(session)` (the session's override, else the workspace setting) so they always agree: the block-0 persona, the block-1 org block, and the tool list, which drops `send_company_broadcast`, `send_department_message` and `set_department_head` *before* the sort, so it stays sorted and keeps its 1h marker on the last tool. The resolved mode is pinned on the session for the rest of the turn, so the tool handlers use it too and a switch made mid-turn applies from the next turn. Every part is a constant or stable per install, so each mode keeps its own warm cache and switching modes misses once.

The two personas share most of their text. `prompts/executive_persona.py` holds plain string literals — a shared head, body and tail plus team or solo sections — concatenated at import and never formatted, so both prompts are constants. The team prompt is byte-for-byte what it was before the split; a test pins its sha256.

Tool schemas are static: nothing in a definition depends on company data — `create_goal` takes its area as optional free text and its owner as a plain `owner_person_id`, rather than enums of the current departments or people, which would change the cached tool prefix every time an area was added, and `record_decision_outcome` takes a plain decision id. The solo persona is still one constant: its goal and decision-outcome lines (`_SOLO_CREATE_GOAL`, `_SOLO_DECISION_OUTCOME`) are literals concatenated at import, and the team persona is byte-identical (a test pins its sha256). The scheduler's proactive-trigger run (a Session marked `unattended`), a turn private to the principal (`Session.private_to_principal`: mail from one of their contacts, or mail they forwarded), a read-only turn and a shared chat a teammate wrote into are all sent the same list as any other turn in their mode: the tools `schedule_tools.UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS` and `PRIVATE_TURN_WITHHELD_TOOLS` name stay offered, and the one check (`orchestrator.levels`) runs or holds a call to them at dispatch, so none of these turns changes the cached tool prefix. Only a missing Python sandbox (fixed per process) and a replay of a graded turn drop tools before the sort. Act as me adds tools rather than dropping any: on a turn `delegation.settings.pin_turn_delegation` offered it to (the principal's own verified, attended turn in a private conversation, with it on), `ghostwrite_email`, the mailbox and calendar reads (`search_my_email`, `read_my_email`, `read_my_email_attachment`, `my_email_awaiting_reply`, `my_email_read_before`, `my_calendar`, and `save_my_email_attachment`, which copies a file out of it), `remind_me` and `propose_actions` join the pool together before the sort, so those turns share one more sorted prefix and every other turn's list is byte-identical to before. The offer never depends on the Gmail connection, so a lapsed token never flips the prefix. `recall_history` (Always in the loop) joins the same way, before the sort, on a turn whose speaker may read their own notes; its offer reads only their switch and the surface, never the notes themselves. The chat note-taker runs after the turn, outside the cached prompt. Tool definitions are sorted by name so their serialized order is stable across requests; the `web_search` server tool (Anthropic direct and OpenRouter) is appended after the sorted list, so it receives no `cache_control` marker. It stays on a private or mail-touched turn, since the tools open the prefix every later marker caches and dropping it would miss it. `web_fetch` is the client-side tool on every model (never Anthropic's server fetch; see Request Lifecycle), an ordinary client tool that sorts into the list like any other, as the SearXNG search does on a local model; it is in `PRIVATE_TURN_WITHHELD_TOOLS` and the Act as me lockdown, so on a private or mail-touched turn the one check (`orchestrator.levels`) runs or holds a call to it at dispatch by the owner's safety level (see Delegation), without changing the list, and a deployment with `WEB_FETCH_MAX_USES=0` simply never has it. The last client tool carries the third marker (1h TTL).

## Tools opened on demand

The less common tools are not in the list at all. `orchestrator.tool_groups` puts them in named groups — calendar, people, memory, corrections, goals, watch_and_alerts, workflows, documents, app, messaging — and `tool_groups.split` takes them out of the turn's offered tools after every filter above (mode, a missing sandbox, a replay) and before the sort, adding two small tools in their place: `open_tools(group)`, whose description names each offered group and its tools, and `use_tool(name, input)`. When the model opens a group, the loop answers with that group's tools (name, description, input schema) as a **tool result**. It never adds them to the list: the list is the start of the cached prefix, so a list that grew mid-turn would miss the cache for the tools, both system blocks and the whole history. The list is the same on every call of every turn, and a group's descriptions are paid for only on a turn that opens it. That took the direct list from about 19,500 tokens to about 6,500, re-sent on every model call.

`open_tools`'s description and its results name only the tools the turn offers (`tool_groups.open_tools_tool`), so a turn never sees the name of a tool it is not offered. The description depends only on that set, which is fixed for each kind of turn, so each still has one stable list. A `use_tool` call is rewritten into the tool's own call, same id, before dispatch (`tool_groups.unwrap`); the model's assistant block stays as it was sent, so the result pairs with the id it used. The rewritten call meets the same guards, handler, progress events and audit rows as a direct call. `use_tool` takes only names in `tool_groups.DEFERRED`; anything else, or an input that is not an object, gets an error tool result. The everyday tools (`consult_specialist`, `propose_form_values`, `read_user_guide`, `message_person`, `lookup_person`, `list_people`, `remember_fact`, `keep_figure`, follow-ups, the MCP meta-tools) stay direct. The rarely used `ask_about_person` (people), `forget_fact` and `update_company_profile` (memory) sit in groups, which keeps about 5,000 characters of descriptions off every call.

The routing pre-pass is the one turn-level exception to a single stable tool list. It reuses the same system blocks as the main turn but offers only `consult_specialist`, so it is a different cached prefix — it does not warm the main turn's tool block and the main turn does not warm it. Measured locally the cost is small (about 0.4 s of extra prompt processing on a 27B model, against a 0.27 s warm main turn), because the divergence is in the tool block rather than in the much larger persona and profile blocks. Its one tool does carry a 1h marker of its own, so the pre-pass prefix is cached too. Both figures were measured before `tool_groups` moved the less common tools behind `open_tools` (above), which shrank the main turn's own tool block; the pre-pass's own prefix is unchanged. It buys routing that otherwise does not happen; `ROUTING_PREPASS_ENABLED=false` removes both the call and its cache cost.

## The intra-turn marker

The fourth and final breakpoint belongs to the tool-use loop. After each iteration appends its `tool_result` blocks, `executive._apply_loop_cache_marker` moves a single ephemeral marker onto the **newest non-empty tool result**. Without it the loop caches only the static tools+system prefix, so every iteration re-sends the whole accumulated transcript at full input price — the runtime signature is `cache_read_input_tokens` pinned flat while the prompt grows iteration over iteration.

The marker **moves rather than accumulates**: each pass first sweeps every `tool_result` clean, then re-marks the newest one. A marker left in place per iteration would reach one breakpoint per round and blow the 4-block limit. Sweeping first also makes the helper idempotent — there is no bookkeeping index to drift.

On the loop's **first call** there is no tool result yet, so the same slot marks the **message being answered** instead (`executive._mark_turn_message`, 5m): the question plus this turn's context (facts, memory, knowledge excerpts). Without it the first call sends that context uncached and the second call writes the same tokens to the cache, so it is paid twice; with it the first call writes it once and later calls read it back. The marker sits on a copy of the message, never the caller's dict, and comes off (`_clear_turn_marker`) as soon as the loop marker lands on a tool result, so a request never carries both.

## The history marker

Once a conversation has history, the agent loop also marks the **newest non-empty history turn** (normally the previous reply) with a **1h** breakpoint (`executive._apply_history_cache_marker`), so the next message reads the whole conversation back from cache and writes only what is new: the last exchange, this turn's context and its tool calls. History turns are rebuilt from plain text, so the previous turn's loop entries, which ended inside that turn's retrieved context and tool results, never match; without this marker every message re-wrote the whole conversation into the cache. 1h because people reply in minutes, not seconds.

The history marker takes the company block's slot: block 1 stays in the prefix, covered by the history marker, and dropping its 5m marker keeps the TTLs in the order the API requires, longer before shorter. On a first message (no history) block 1 keeps its 5m marker as before. `_build_messages` itself never marks history, so the committee revision call, which reuses those messages, keeps the plain layout. `Session.get_recent_history` moves its window's start in steps of 10 turns (keeping 20 to 30), so a long conversation's first history message, and the cached prefix with it, stays put between steps instead of shifting every turn. On the OpenRouter path the translator keeps assistant turns as typed text parts whenever a request carries the history marker (`translator._request_caches_assistant_text`), so the marker reaches Anthropic and every reply has the same shape whether or not it is the one marked. A rolling marker on every history turn used to claim a latent fifth breakpoint, which Anthropic rejects outright.

**The breakpoint budget, in full:** last client tool (1h) + persona+knowledge (1h) + company+org (5m, first message only) or history (1h) + the turn's message on the first call, then the newest tool result (5m) = at most 4, longer TTLs first.

RAG context is **never** placed in a cached system block — retrieved hits vary per query and would poison the cache. It is injected into the **user turn** instead. The chat surfaces (web chat, Telegram, Discord, Google Chat) cap it at `KNOWLEDGE_CHAT_MAX_CHARS` (default 6,000 characters, 0 = no cap): `retriever._fit_to_budget` keeps the closest chunks across every collection until the cap, because each excerpt is re-sent on every call of the turn.

Specialist calls follow the same rule. Each specialist caches only its static domain prompt (`BaseAgent.analyze`, one ephemeral block); everything per call — retrieved knowledge, failure cases, past decisions, department memory, the company's stage (`<company_stage>`) and, in solo mode, the principal's role (`<principal_role>`) — goes in the specialist's user turn, so the cached domain prompt is byte-identical across companies and profile edits.

The ghostwriter's call (Act as me) carries no cache markers: its system prompt is the constant `GHOSTWRITER_PROMPT` plus that person's voice block — short, and sent only when a draft is written — and the thread and the intent go in its user turn.

## Tool-result bound

Read sizes come from the turn's model, not from a setting (`providers.registry.reading_limits_for`, from `providers.feature_gate.context_tokens`): a turn's reads may fill 40% of the model's window at 3 characters a token, up to 200,000 characters (`feature_gate.MAX_TURN_READ_CHARS`, the owner's cost limit; a 1M-token Claude or Haiku 4.5 is held to that, a self-hosted model may get less from `LOCAL_CONTEXT_TOKENS`), and one part of one read is half that, so an ordinary long document fits whole or in two parts. Each result is sized at the one point every result reaches the model (`orchestrator.reading.TurnReadingBudget`, which a workflow action step uses too) rather than at each producer — so it also covers specialist output, tool errors and the unknown-tool fallback, while non-model consumers (the `propose_form_values` JSON parse, the audit trail) still read the full text. A longer result comes back in parts: the first ends in a marker naming the tool and both character counts and saying to repeat the call with the same input, and that repeat is answered with the next part from the result in hand, never by running the tool again (it may have been a write); the last part says it is the last. Only a turn that has read all its model can hold stops short: a further result shows its first 3,000 characters and its note says so plainly, to answer from what it has, say what it has not read and offer to carry on, and never to edit or rewrite anything from the cut result. A specialist's answer is the analysis itself, not a read, so it neither counts nor is cut; a built tool's result (`run_script`) and tool discovery (`open_tools`, `search_tools`) count but are never cut by the turn, since one lists the writes that already ran and the others are the schema the next call needs.

**The invariant:** never put dynamic content in a `cache_control` block. A single mutating value breaks the cache and drives roughly a 10x cost increase.
